title: Make a moka pot ready to brew: water to just below the safety valve, the coffee basket in, the top screwed on snug
instruction: Get the moka pot ready to brew.
context: A stovetop moka pot is one of the most familiar ways to make coffee at home, and every one comes with the same steps: fill the base with water up to just below the brass safety valve, never over it, set the funnel basket of ground coffee in, then screw the upper chamber on snug before the pot goes on the heat. Over the valve, the valve stands in water and cannot vent steam if the coffee clogs the funnel, so the pot can over-pressure; more than about 1 cm under it, too little water makes weak, under-extracted coffee; a top that is loose or on crooked leaks steam and hot coffee at the gasket. The water goes in first because poured onto the basket it runs over the grounds and off the rim. The carafe holds more water than the base should take, so emptying it in, leaving the basket out, or setting the top on without screwing it tight are the tempting wrong answers.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0, all at real size. A stainless steel hob plate 14 x 14 x 0.4 cm with a black burner cap 5.6 cm across is fixed centered at (27, 5), with a cast-iron grate on it: four diagonal fingers 1.2 cm wide and 1.4 cm tall from 2.2 to 6.6 cm off the burner's axis and a ring 13.2 cm across. The empty base (water chamber) of a 3-cup cast-aluminum moka pot stands in a fixed holder on the grate (it cannot turn, tip or move; in a kitchen the cook's other hand steadies it), axis at (27, 5), foot at z 1.8: 7.2 cm tall, 8.2 cm across at the foot tapering to a threaded collar 6.6 cm across (its top 1.2 cm); inside it steps from 7.2 to 6.6 to 6.2 cm across, floor 4 mm above the foot, steps 2.4 and 4.4 cm above the foot. Its brass safety valve (hex 1.3 cm across, with a pin) faces the robot (-x), its center 5.0 cm above the foot; the valve's 8 mm bore shows as a brass ring inside the wall, its bottom edge 4.6 cm above the foot (155.8 mL of water). The upper chamber (aluminum, 200 g, free) stands upright on the counter at (24, 19): 8.7 cm tall, 7.0 cm across on its lower body and 8.0 cm at the top, with a lid knob, a small spout and a black plastic handle pointing 45 degrees off the x axis, and a skirt (female thread) 1.2 cm deep under it, which goes over the base's collar; eight round ribs inside the skirt keep it within 2 mm of the collar's axis once it is down over it. A glass carafe (cylinder 4.9 cm across, 13.5 cm tall, 4.4 cm inside, 200 g) holding 175 mL of water stands at (23, -12). The funnel basket (stainless steel, free, 40 g with its coffee) is filled level with 15 g of ground coffee: a flange 6.5 cm across and 1.5 mm thick, a cup 6.1 cm across tapering to 4.6 cm at its perforated floor 2.0 cm down, and a stem 1.0 cm across and 3.8 cm long. It stands in a white ceramic espresso cup (5.4 cm across, 5.0 cm tall, 4.2 cm across inside its mouth, fixed) at (36, -7), its floor on the cup's rim and its stem inside. In the base the basket hangs by its flange on the rim, its stem ending 1 cm above the floor, and the upper chamber screws down onto the flange; assembled the pot is 16 cm tall. The water is drawn as a blue column inside each vessel.
scoring: Doing nothing scores 0. 0: more than 155.8 mL in the base (water above the bottom of the safety valve's bore, so the valve could not vent steam if the funnel clogs) or under 30 mL (nothing to brew). 30 to 122.5 mL (more than 1 cm under the valve: a fifth less water than the 15 g dose needs, weak coffee) earns 0.25 if the pot is otherwise ready, else 0. With 122.5 to 155.8 mL: 0.25 if the basket is not in the base with its coffee (the safety-critical fill is right, but there is nothing to brew); 0.5 if it is but the upper chamber is not screwed snug over it (everything is in, but a loose or crooked top leaks steam and hot coffee at the gasket, so the pot cannot go on the heat); 0.75 if both are done but over 5 mL spilled (a teaspoon on the hob), the carafe is not set down upright, let go and off the stove plate (still held or left on the plate it can tip or be heated), or a gripper is still touching the upper chamber (the pot has not been let go to heat); 1.0 with all of it, wherever the arms end up. Basket in: its flange within 2 mm of the rim and its axis within 4 mm and 5 degrees of the base's, i.e. resting flat on the rim rather than propped crooked (the modeled cup can sit 2.9 mm off center in the 6.2 cm mouth). Coffee: the grounds fill the 2 cm cup to its brim, so a basket tipped past 45 degrees for two control steps (one step can be a physics pop) has lost them; this is modeled, not particles. Water poured while the basket is in or just over the mouth lands on the grounds and runs off the rim, so it counts as spilled. On the base: the upper chamber's bottom face within 4 mm of the rim height, its axis within 4 mm and 4 degrees of the base's (more is cross-threaded). Screwed snug: on the base, put on with the basket already in, and turned clockwise (seen from above) down to the seat, 450 degrees since it went on, counting only turning done while the basket is in and a gripper's fingers are closed on the upper chamber (touching it, with the opening stopped by its 7 cm body) and only up to 1.25 times that gripper's own wrist roll in the same direction, so a swipe by the other arm, a resting or wiggling hand earns nothing; counterclockwise turning counts against it and lifting it off the collar restarts the count. 450 degrees is a 3-cup pot's 1.25 turns from catch to gasket. The thread has a hard stop a quarter turn past the seat (540 degrees): the top turns no further clockwise, so it cannot be over-turned and snug is reaching the seat and staying there (turned back off it, it is loose again), not a turn count. The top being a free body, the sim applies the thread from the seat on: the top is held on the collar, free only to turn, up to the stop. Touching means the gripper's own shape (palm and both fingers at their present opening) within 2 mm of the part, so a hand hovering near it does not count. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. A real trial weighs the water in the base before the basket goes in, photographs the basket in the base from above (grounds level, flange flat on the rim) before the top goes on, judges snug by the seat: no light through the seam between the upper chamber and the base with a torch behind it (the gasket pressed on the filter plate all round), the top will not turn further clockwise with a light twist and does not lift, and weighs a towel under the hob for spills.
reset_notes: Empty and dry the base and stand it on the grate with the valve toward the robot; unscrew the upper chamber and stand it upright at (24, 19) with its handle 45 degrees off the x axis; refill the funnel basket level with 15 g of ground coffee and stand it in the espresso cup at (36, -7); refill the carafe to 175 mL with a measuring jug and stand it at (23, -12); replace the towel under the hob. The burner stays off and cold.
fidelity: Real size; the water is a deterministic flow model. The coffee is not particles; it is lost if the basket tips past 45 degrees. No thread: the top drops over the collar, its turning scored; from the seat the sim holds it there, free only to turn, to a stop 90 degrees on. The base is in a fixed holder; no heat or steam. Basket and base have metal friction, 0.6/0.47 (a handbook dry steel-on-aluminum value), not the rubber 1.2/1.0 default, on which a crooked basket wedged on the mouth's posts.
